raw_responses.Bulgarian: DESCRIPTION: The figure is a semi-log plot showing the relationship between sparsity rate and perplexity for two methods: Per-Output and Per-Layer. The x-axis represents the sparsity rate, ranging from 10% to 80% in increments of 10%, with a linear scale. The y-axis represents perplexity, labeled with values from $10^1$ to $10^3$ on a logarithmic scale. There are two data series, one for Per-Output (blue) and one for Per-Layer (orange). Both series start at a perplexity value slightly above $10^1$ at 10% sparsity and increase gradually until 70%, where perplexity sharply increases to around $10^1$ for both, and then drastically rises to just below $10^3$ at 80% sparsity. Notably, the perplexity values for both methods are very similar at lower sparsity rates but diverge significantly at higher rates, particularly at 80%. The plot does not provide specific numerical values for perplexity at each sparsity rate but illustrates a clear trend of increasing perplexity with increasing sparsity rate, with an accelerated increase after 70%.
raw_responses.Chinese:
The figure presents a bar chart illustrating the relationship between sparsity rate and perplexity for two categories: Per-Output and Per-Layer. 

The horizontal axis represents the sparsity rate, labeled with percentages from 10% to 80% in increments of 10%. The vertical axis, labeled "Perplexity," is on a logarithmic scale, ranging from $10^1$ to $10^3$, with ticks at $10^1$, $10^2$, and $10^3$. 

Two series of bars are plotted: Per-Output in blue and Per-Layer in orange. For Per-Output, the perplexity values are approximately 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 10, 20, and 600, corresponding to sparsity rates of 10% through 80%, respectively. For Per-Layer, the perplexity values are roughly 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 12, 50, and 1000, corresponding to the same sparsity rates.

The bars for both categories generally increase in height as the sparsity rate increases, with a more pronounced increase at higher sparsity rates, particularly above 60%. There is no explicit grouping or stacking of bars; each category has its distinct set of bars. The bars are not sorted in any specific order other than corresponding to their respective sparsity rates. No bars are visually emphasized through shading, bolding, or outlining. 

DESCRIPTION: The figure is a bar chart showing the perplexity of two categories, Per-Output and Per-Layer, across different sparsity rates from 10% to 80%. The vertical axis is on a logarithmic scale, and both series show an increase in perplexity with increasing sparsity rate, with a more significant rise at higher rates.
raw_responses.English:
The chart illustrates the relationship between sparsity rate and perplexity for two categories, "Per-Output" and "Per-Layer". The horizontal axis represents the sparsity rate, labeled with percentages from 10% to 80% in increments of 10%, with no indicated units. The vertical axis represents perplexity, labeled with values ranging from $10^1$ to $10^3$ on a logarithmic scale, with no specified units. The "Per-Output" category is depicted by blue bars, while the "Per-Layer" category is represented by orange bars. At the lowest sparsity rate of 10%, both categories have a perplexity of approximately $5$. As the sparsity rate increases, the perplexity for both categories generally increases; notably, at 80% sparsity, the perplexity for "Per-Output" is around $600$ and for "Per-Layer" is around $800$. The bars are not sorted in any specific order other than corresponding to increasing sparsity rates, and there is no visual emphasis on any particular bar. The chart does not group or stack bars but presents them side-by-side for comparison across different sparsity rates.
